title: Prince Harry and Co-Claimants Ordered to Pay Up to £34.5m in Privacy Case Costs
summary:
Prince Harry and six other high-profile figures are facing a staggering legal bill after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional costs order in their failed privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail. The group could be liable for up to £34.5 million—far exceeding the £16.2 million their insurance was set to cover—after Mr. Justice Nicklin ruled their claims were presented in a manner "unreasonable to a high degree."

The case, which was dismissed on July 7, alleged unlawful information-gathering by Associated Newspapers. The claimants—including Sir Elton John, David Furnish, Sir Simon Hughes, Baroness Lawrence, Sadie Frost, and Liz Hurley—had accused the publisher of serious wrongdoing. However, the judge noted that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group, a fact he found "striking." He said such allegations "cannot properly be left hanging over individuals" and that the claimants' failure to withdraw them was "not a proper or disciplined way to deal with serious allegations."

Justice Nicklin acknowledged that a claim for costs exceeding £34 million appeared "excessive" and raised concerns about whether all costs were reasonably incurred. Yet he declined to impose a ceiling, saying it would be "too broad-brushed" and risk unfairness. He also ruled that costs should be assessed on an indemnity basis, which is more favorable to the publisher.

In a statement, Associated Newspapers called the ruling "a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives." Prince Harry and Baroness Lawrence, in a joint statement after last month's judgment, said: "We came to court seeking justice and accountability. But we have received neither."

The claimants have until October 2 to seek permission to appeal. The ruling comes days after Prince Harry and Meghan announced plans to return to the UK with their children, who are enrolled to start school in September. The financial stakes are enormous, and the case serves as a stark reminder of the risks of high-stakes litigation.
why_it_matters: The ruling shows how high-stakes privacy lawsuits can produce enormous financial consequences for public figures when a court decides claims were handled improperly, raising deeper questions about the balance between holding the media accountable and discouraging weak litigation.

background_read: Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, is the younger son of King Charles III; he and his wife Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, stepped back from royal duties in 2020 and have repeatedly sued British newspapers over privacy.
The High Court is one of the senior courts in England and Wales, hearing high-value and complex civil cases including defamation and privacy claims.
Associated Newspapers Limited publishes the Daily Mail, a widely read British newspaper, and has faced multiple legal challenges from public figures over journalistic methods.
In English civil litigation, the losing party generally pays the winning party's legal costs, but an indemnity basis is stricter and can lead to higher awards.

The case follows a long-running pattern of celebrities and public figures using privacy law to challenge alleged phone hacking and unlawful information-gathering, especially in the British tabloid press.

perspectives.description: Associated Newspapers sees the ruling as a forceful defense of its journalists and a warning against using lawsuits to damage a newspaper's reputation. The publisher argues the judgment protects editors and executives from expensive but weak accusations.

The claimants and privacy campaigners argue the outcome denies accountability and imposes punishing costs on people who sought to expose unlawful information-gathering. They worry that such financial risk can silence public figures who try to challenge powerful media organizations.

Legal analysts note that English courts have wide discretion in costs, and the use of an indemnity basis signals strong judicial disapproval. The judge's refusal to set a ceiling also shows how difficult it is to predict final costs in complex multi-party litigation.

An appeal could affect how future privacy claims are argued and how courts handle serious allegations that are not withdrawn. The case also lands as Prince Harry and Meghan plan a return to the UK with their children, so the final cost and any appeal may shape the family's legal and public strategy.
